title: Revelation and Interpretation in Rabbinic, Philosophical, and Mystical Literature
heading: REL 19.41 Revelation and Interpretation in Rabbinic, Philosophical, and Mystical Literature
description: The course will be dedicated to in-depth readings of primary Jewish texts from Late Antiquity to Modernity. We will study sources from the rabbinic, philosophical, kabbalistic, and Hasidic corpora. Topics to be discussed include the interplay between interpretation and revelation; the ideal of the sage and the practical application of wisdom through law and ritual; the rabbinic conception of dreams as text; the mediation of the universal and the particular and the philosophical critique of philosophy; negative theology and the limits of human understanding; the mystical ideal of ecstatic union and prophecy; the role of metaphor in envisioning the invisible; the convergence of messianism and mysticism; and the pietistic emphasis on worship and communion with the divine.

title: Race and Religion: Jews, Christians, and Colonialism
heading: JWST 13.01 Race and Religion: Jews, Christians, and Colonialism
description: Where does the notion of “race” come from? Is religion a source of racial oppression or a tool for social liberation? This course considers the historic role that scriptural exegesis and religious ideologies have played in the construction of racial categories– ideas that have been used to sacralize slavery, genocide, and colonial conquest for centuries—and conversely, the role of religion in dismantling racial hierarchies in the post-colonial period. We begin with a substantial unit on the racialization of Judaism and then turn to a series of comparative case studies engaging primarily Christian, but also Hindu, Muslim, and Native American contexts. Utilizing a global approach, we will read anthropological, historical, literary, and theological writings to consider the dynamic interaction of religion and race. This course will also challenge students to speak and write critically about contemporary racial justice struggles from a religious studies perspective.
